gate: Opinions form here before anyone asks for one. Watch a person carrying this code in a room when the group cannot decide where to eat. They already know what they think. The thought arrived clean, with a shape, and now sits in the mouth wanting out. This is the code that produces a point of view as easily as a body produces breath. The misread is to confuse opinions with answers. An opinion is a pattern noticed and named, not a fact about how things will turn out. It is a logical guess that wants to be tested in conversation, sharpened, sometimes shifted. The trouble starts when the opinion is gripped as if it were certainty, defended like territory, pressed onto people who did not ask. Held lightly, the same code is fair, clear, useful. Held tight, it becomes righteousness with good vocabulary.
centre_field: The Ajna is the body's processing centre, the upside-down triangle that sits between the head and the throat. Its job is not to decide anything. Its job is to take in raw input from the head and sort it, pattern it, make it usable. Information goes in noisy and comes out shaped. Placing this code there means opinions are the form the sorting takes. Logic looks at what has happened, finds the recurring shape, and offers it back as a position. Notice the placement: the centre between the question and the voice. The opinion has been processed before it gets spoken, which is why it arrives so confidently formed. The risk of the placement is that an awareness centre is mistaken for a decision centre. The Ajna analyses brilliantly. It is not the part of the body that knows what to do.
channel: Picture the opinion sitting in the Ajna with nowhere to land. It has shape, it has logic, but it lacks the granular evidence that would let another person actually use it. This code reaches toward the gate of details, and the two together form the channel of acceptance. The reach is what makes the difference. Details are the specifics, the particulars, the concrete instances a pattern was drawn from. Without them, an opinion is just a strong feeling dressed in logic. With them, the opinion can be examined, accepted, argued with on terms. The detail half is what makes the position legible. Alone, this code generates positions that sound certain and float free. Joined, the positions land. The opinion becomes something a listener can pick up, weigh, decide what to do with. The code is built to need its evidence.
